This view is mistaken, because reports (akhbar) are not abrogated. We mention this view only to draw attention to its falsity.

The words of God, Mighty and Majestic:

﴿About what are they asking one another?﴾ ﴿About the momentous news,﴾ ﴿concerning which they differ.﴾ ﴿No! They will come to know.﴾ ﴿Again, no! They will come to know.﴾ ﴿Have We not made the earth a bed,﴾ ﴿and the mountains as pegs?﴾ ﴿And We created you in pairs,﴾ ﴿and We made your sleep a rest,﴾ ﴿and We made the night a covering,﴾ ﴿and We made the day for livelihood,﴾ ﴿and We built above you seven strong (heavens),﴾ ﴿and We made a blazing lamp,﴾ ﴿and We sent down from the rain-laden clouds abundant water,﴾ ﴿that We may bring forth thereby grain and plants,﴾ ﴿and gardens of thick growth.﴾

The origin of ʿamma ("about what") is ʿan mā ("about what"). Then the nun was assimilated into the mim after being changed, so ʿammā remained, both in the declarative and in the interrogative. Then they dropped the alif in the interrogative to distinguish it from the declarative. Then among the Arabs there are those who lighten the mim, saying ʿamma (ʿamma). This interrogation with ʿamma is an interrogation of reproach and wonder on their part. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Ibn Masʿud, ʿIkrima and ʿIsa read ʿammā with an alif. Al-Dahhak read ʿammah with a hāʾ, and this occurs only in pausal pronunciation (waqf).

As for "the momentous news": some people said it is the Law (shariʿa) which Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. Mujahid and Qatada said it is the Qur'an specifically. Qatada also said it is the Resurrection from the graves. The pronoun in "they ask one another" may refer to all of creation, in which case "the difference" means the believers' affirmation, the disbelievers' denial, and the doubts of the atheists. It may also refer to the disbelievers of Quraysh, in which case "the difference" means that some doubt and some deny, and their saying that it is magic, soothsaying, madness, and other things. The words of God, Exalted is He, ﴿about the momentous news﴾ are connected to the apparent "they ask one another," as if He, Exalted is He, said: why do they ask about this news?

Al-Zajjaj said: the speech is complete at the words of God, Exalted is He, ﴿About what are they asking one another?﴾. Then the expected form of the speech would be that a respondent answers, "They ask one another about the momentous news." But the concision of the Qur'an, with its eloquence, requires that the one making the argument hasten to the answer that the situation and the context call for, in brevity of argument and hurrying to the point where they are cut off. This is like the words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest as testimony?" Say: "God is the witness."﴾ [Al-Anʿam: 19]. There are many examples of this, and attention has been drawn to them in their places.

The Seven (readers), al-Hasan, Abu Jaʿfar, Shayba and al-Aʿmash read ﴿Nay! They will come to know﴾ with yāʾ in both places, as a reference to the third person. The apparent meaning of the speech is that it is a rejection of the disbelievers in their denial and a threat to them in the future. He repeated the rebuke for emphasis. Al-Dahhak said the meaning is: "No! They will come to know," meaning the disbelievers, as a threat; "Again, no! They will come to know," meaning the believers, as a promise. Ibn ʿAmir (according to what was narrated from him), Malik ibn Dinar and al-Hasan (in one report) read ﴿Nay! They will come to know﴾ with tāʾ in both places, addressing the one present, as if He, Exalted is He, were saying: "Say to them, O Muhammad, and repeat the rebuke and the promise to them for emphasis." Every interpretation of this reading other than this is forced. Some read ﴿Nay! They will come to know﴾ with yāʾ, as a rejection and threat to the disbelievers, then ﴿Nay! They will come to know﴾ with tāʾ from above, as a rejection of the disbelievers and a promise to the believers. In this verse, "to know" has the meaning of "you will recognize," which is why it takes no object.

Then God, Exalted is He, made them stand before His signs, the wonders of His creatures, and His power, the contemplation of which necessitates acknowledgment of the Resurrection and faith in God, Exalted is He. Al-mihad is a bed prepared for treading, and the earth is likewise because of its structure. Mujahid, ʿIsa and some of the Kufans read mahdan, and the meaning is close to the first. He compared the mountains to pegs because they hold fast, are heavy, and prevent the earth from swaying. Azwajan means kinds, in your colors, forms and languages. Some said it means "in pairs," male and female.

As-subat is stillness. "Sabata al-rajulu" means he rested, ceased, and left off work. From it comes subat, which is a known illness, so named because stillness or silence overcomes a person until it becomes harmful and deadly. Sleep resembles it except in harm. Abu ʿUbayda said: subatan means cessation of works and activity. As-sabt is cutting, and from it comes "sabt al-rajul shaʿrahu" (he cut his hair) when his hair is cut. From it also come the sabtiyya sandals, which are those from which the hair (of the hide) has been cut off.

Libas is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and the night is like this in that it covers persons, so they are clothed in it and wrapped in it. It is also said: He made it a covering because it obscures the light of sight and confuses things for the eyes. The morphology weakens this view, because it should have been malbas (a garment), and libas is said only of one who wears clothes. ﴿And We made the day for livelihood﴾ is either by omission of a modifier, or by way of attribution (nisba), like saying "a sleeping night" (laylun nāʾim). The seven strong (heavens) are the skies. The more eloquent usage of the word samāʾ is feminine. He described them as strong because corruption does not quickly reach them, owing to their firmness. As-sirāj is the sun. Al-wahhāj is the hot, blazing, intensely kindled, with high flames. ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs said: the sun in the fourth heaven, its back is toward us, and its flame is blazing high.

People differed about al-muʿṣirāt. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Ibn Jubayr, Zayd ibn Aslam, Muqatil and Qatada said they are the heavens. Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu al-ʿAliya, al-Rabiʿ and al-Dahhak said al-muʿṣirāt are the clouds that drip. It is derived from ʿaṣr (pressing), because the cloud is pressed and water comes out of it. This is the view of the majority, and al-Hasan ibn Muhammad al-ʿAnbari al-Qadi explained the verse of Hassan with it:

"Both of them are the milking of the pressed juice..."

The verse.

Some of those who were named said: they are the clouds in which there is water but which have not yet rained, like the pregnant woman (al-muʿṣir), who is one whose menses are near but who has not yet menstruated. Ibn Kaysan said: the clouds were called muʿṣirāt because they give relief (tughīthu), so they are from ʿaṣra (relief), and from this is the words of God, Exalted is He: "and in it they will be given relief (yaʿṣirūn)" [Yusuf: 49]. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Mujahid said: al-muʿṣirāt are the winds, because they press the clouds. Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Fadl ibn ʿAbbas, Qatada and ʿIkrima read ﴿and We sent down with the muʿṣirāt﴾, and this strengthens the view that He meant the winds. Ath-thajjāj is that which gushes forth rapidly, as blood gushes from the veins of a slaughtered animal. From it comes the words of the Prophet (ﷺ), when he was asked: "What is the best of the Hajj?" He said: "The ʿajj and the thajj," meaning: supplicating loudly and sacrificing the offering (hady). Al-ḥabb is the class of grains which animals benefit from, and al-nabāt is the herbage used fresh for people or beasts. God, Exalted is He, mentioned the place of both benefits. Alfafan is the plural of luff, with a ḍamma on the lām, and luff is the plural of laffāʾ, and the meaning is intertwined branches and leaves, which is always present with freshness and irrigation. Some said alfafan is the plural of lifaf, with a kasra on the lām, and al-laff is a garden intertwined with branches. Al-Kisa'i said alfafan is the plural of lafif, and the poet has said:

"Ahabish of dense clusters, whose branches differ and whose roots are far from the lineage of the one seeking kinship."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 78, verses 17–23:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said:

﴿Indeed, the Day of Judgement is a appointed time.﴾ ﴿The Day the Horn is blown, and you will come forth in multitudes.﴾ ﴿And the heaven will be opened, and it will become gateways.﴾ ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion, and they will become a mirage.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Hell has been lying in wait,﴾ ﴿a dwelling place for the transgressors.﴾ ﴿Remaining therein for ages.﴾

(p-516) "The Day of Decision" (yawm al-fasl) is the Day of Resurrection, because Allah the Exalted decides on that Day between the believers and the disbelievers, and between truth and falsehood. "Al-miqat" (appointed time) is a form of the noun derived from "al-waqt" (time), like "mi'ad" (appointment) from "al-wa'd" (promise). His saying, the Exalted, "The Day the Horn is blown" (yawma yunfakh) is a substitution (badal) for the first "yawm" (day). "Al-Sur" is the horn into which one blows to raise the people, this is the statement of the majority. It is possible in this place that "al-Suwar" is the plural of "suwrah" (form), meaning: the Day on which Allah the Exalted returns the spirits to the bodies. This is the view of some people regarding "al-Suwar," and Abu Hatim permitted it. The first (view) is more well-known, and the narrations corroborate it, and it is the apparent meaning of the Book of Allah the Exalted in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Then it will be blown again﴾ [al-Zumar: 68]. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, read "al-Suwar" with a fatha on the waw.

"Al-Afwaj" are the groups following one another; its singular is "fawj" (group).

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far, Shayba and al-Hasan read "wa-futtihat" with a shadda on the ta, for emphasis. 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "wa-futihat" without a shadda. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿so it will become gateways﴾ — it was said its meaning is: it will split and cleave until there are openings in it like doors in walls. Others said, as transmitted by Makki ibn Abi Talib: "al-abwab" here refers to the split planks of wood that are made into doors for the openings of walls, meaning the sky will be broken into small pieces until it becomes like the panels of doors. The first view is better. Some scholars of knowledge said: doors will open in the sky for the angels, from which they descend and ascend. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿so it will become a mirage﴾ is an expression for its dissolution and annihilation after becoming scattered dust. He, the Exalted, did not intend that the mountains become like water at a distance from the one who looks at them.

"Mirsad" is the place of watching (ar-rasd), and from it is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful﴾ [al-Fajr: 14]. It has been narrated from al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan that he said: No one enters Paradise until he passes over Hell; whoever has means of salvation is saved, and otherwise he perishes. Qatada said: know that there is no path to Paradise until the Fire is crossed. In the authentic hadith: "Indeed the Sirat is a bridge set up over the back of Hell, then people cross over it, some saved and some hurled down." Some interpreters said: "mirsad" is a form (mif'al) with the meaning of (p-517) "watcher" (rasid). Abu Ma'mar al-Minqari read "anna Jahannam" with a fatha on the alif, while the majority read it with a kasra. "Al-taghun" are the disbelievers, and "al-ma'ab" is the return. "Al-ahqab" is the plural of "huqab" with a damma on the ha and a fatha on the qaf, and "huqab" with a kasra on the ha, and "huqub" with a damma on the qaf; it is the plural of "huqbah," from which is the verse of Mutammim:

"And we were like the boon companions of Jadhima for a huqbah of time, until it was said they would never part."

It is a long, unbounded period of time. The word is also used for a year. (p-518) Bishr ibn Ka'b said: its duration, according to what is mentioned in the revealed books, is three hundred years. Hilal al-Hajari said: eighty years, both saying: in each year there are three hundred and sixty days. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them, said: eighty thousand years. Al-Hasan said: seventy thousand years. It was also said: fifty thousand years. Abu Umama reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "It is thirty thousand years." People have multiplied opinions on this. What is necessary is that Allah the Exalted informed about the disbelievers that they will remain for ages, whenever one age passes another comes, without end. Al-Hasan said: it has no count except eternal abiding in the Fire. Some people, because of the mention of ages, thought that the duration of the punishment is limited and finite, so they sought an interpretation for that. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: the huqb is seventeen thousand years, and it is abrogated by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So taste, for We shall increase you only in punishment﴾ [al-Naba': 30]. We have already mentioned the invalidity of this view. Others said: those described as remaining for ages are the sinful believers. This is also weak, and what follows in the surah indicates against it. Others said: the meaning is only: remaining therein for ages, not tasting coolness or drink; in this state they remain for ages, then the punishment remains everlasting while they drink the drinks of Hell.

The majority read "labithin," while Hamza alone, Ibn Mas'ud, 'Alqama, Ibn Wathhab, 'Amr ibn Maymun, and 'Amr ibn Shurahbil read "labithin," the plural of "labith." This reading is problematic, because the form fa'il is used only for what has become an innate characteristic, like "hadhir" and "fariq," and it has come anomalously in what is not innate. Al-Tabari and others cited the verse of Labid in this regard:

"Or a swift, sturdy wild ass, a flanking of a smooth-backed she-camel, with a scar and wounds on its back."

(p-519) The objector to the reading said: there is no proof in this verse, because "'amal" (doer) has become like an innate quality, one who constantly practices work so that he is named by it even at a time when he is not working, just as you say "katib" (writer) for one who has the profession even if he does not write most of the time. The one who argued for the reading said: "labatha" resembles, through its permanence, the innate quality, since remaining is part of its nature.

Among their sayings is: "Coolness (al-bard) prevented coolness (al-bard)." The majority of scholars said: "al-bard" in the verse means the touch of cold air, which is al-qarr; that is, they will not be touched by anything from it that gives pleasure and breaks the torment of heat. His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿On the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in rows, none shall speak except one whom the Most Merciful permits, and who says what is right.﴾ ﴿That Day is the Truth, so whoever wills may take a return to his Lord.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment, the Day when a man will look at what his hands have sent forward, and the disbeliever will say, "Would that I were dust!"﴾

Scholars have differed about the "Spirit" mentioned in this passage. Al-Sha'bi and al-Dahhak said it is Jibril, peace be upon him, and he was singled out for mention from among the angels as an honour. Ibn Mas'ud said it is a great angel, the largest of the angels in creation, called "the Spirit." Ibn Zayd said: "My father used to say it is the Qur'an," and Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a Spirit of Our command﴾ [al-Shura: 52].

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Standing (qiyam) here is used figuratively, meaning its manifestation, its appearance, and the intensity of its effects, and the things that result from affirming or denying it. Yet with this interpretation there is some strain. Mujahid said: "The Spirit is a creation in the form of the children of Adam; they eat and drink." Ibn 'Abbas, reporting from the Prophet ﷺ, said: "The Spirit is a creation other than the angels, and they are guardians for the angels, just as the angels are guardians for the prophets and for us." Ikrima said: meaning, one who said it in the world.

As for His saying, the Exalted: "That Day is the Truth" (al-haqq), that is, its being and its existence are true. In His saying: ﴿so whoever wills may take a return to his Lord⟩ there is a promise, a threat, and an exhortation. "Ma'ab" means the place of return and the destination of coming back. The pronoun, the kaf and mim in "andharnakum" (We have warned you), is for the whole world, even though the address is directed to the disbelievers who were present with the Prophet ﷺ. As for His saying: ﴿and the disbeliever will say, "Would that I were dust!"⟩, it has been said that this is a wish to be something insignificant that is not called to account and is not attended to. This is indeed found among the fearful believers: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Would that I were a dung-pellet!" Abu Hurayra and 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: Allah the Exalted will bring the animals together on the Day of Resurrection, and He will settle the dispute of some of them against others. Then He will say to them afterward: "Become dust," and all of them will become dust. When the disbelievers see that, they will wish to be like it. Abu al-Qasim ibn Habib said: I saw in some tafsir works that the disbeliever here is Iblis, who, when he sees the reward that the believing children of Adam have obtained, will say: "Would that I were dust," meaning like Adam, who was created from dust and whom he had first despised.

(p-524)

The tafsir (interpretation) of [Surat al-Naba'] is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
